Q: Compiling C/GTK within Eclipse A:

A way to Compile and Link GTK in Eclipse

Executive Summary:
Make two edits in Properties (see steps 13 & 14) to tell Eclipse how to compile and link your GTK project.

My Setup
    Debian Linux
    Eclipse Version 2026-06 (4.40.0) IDE for C/C++ Developers

Prerequisites
    Have installed gtk4 via pkg-config.
    Successfully compiled and linked a gtk4 hello world program via the terminal command line.

1) Create: File -> New -> Project -> C/C++ -> C/C++ Project -> Next
2) Classic C Project -> Next
3) Give the project a name.
4) If not already checked, check "Use default location"
5) For "Project type" choose "Hello World ANSI C Project"
6) For "Toolchains" select "Linux GCC". 
7) Click "Finish"
8) In "Project Explorer" expand the folder with your project name
8) Copy the GTK "Hello World" C file, possibly from 
    https://www.gtk.org/docs/getting-started/hello-world
9) Expand src and double click the "project name.c" file to open it
10) Select all of the .c file source code and paste over it with GTK "Hello World" code
11) Save the .c file
12) Click "Project" dropdown, click "Properties", expand "C/C++ Build, click "Settings"
13) Click "GCC C Compiler". 
"Expert settings: Command line pattern:" reads:
${COMMAND} ${FLAGS} ${OUTPUT_FLAG} ${OUTPUT_PREFIX}${OUTPUT} ${INPUTS} ${EXTRA_FLAGS}
Edit this to read:
${COMMAND} ${shell pkg-config --cflags gtk4} ${FLAGS} ${OUTPUT_FLAG} ${OUTPUT_PREFIX}${OUTPUT} ${INPUTS} ${EXTRA_FLAGS}

14) Click "GCC C Linker"
"Expert settings: Command line pattern:" reads:
${COMMAND} ${FLAGS} ${OUTPUT_FLAG} ${OUTPUT_PREFIX}${OUTPUT} ${INPUTS} ${EXTRA_FLAGS}
Edit this to read:
${COMMAND} ${FLAGS} ${OUTPUT_FLAG} ${OUTPUT_PREFIX}${OUTPUT} ${INPUTS} ${EXTRA_FLAGS} ${shell pkg-config --libs gtk4}
pwdNotes:
Keep the white spacing as it is. The spacing carries through to the GCC command.
Also keep the order of the ${...} commands. The compiler flags ("cflags") are placed following the GCC command because when compilation is successfully completed, linking is performed (I believe eclipse calls the ld command). If the libraries ("libs") are placed earlier in the order, they'll go to the compiler instead of the linker. 

"shell" in the added command causes expansion of the package before it is sent to the compiler or linker.

The ${...} syntax is the modern form of the old `...` backtick syntax. They are very similar in effect. 

Learn a bit more (optional): Run "pkg-config --cflags gtk4" and "pkg-config --libs gtk4" from your Linux terminal command line.

Q: Filter out rows from a DataFrame if value in columns X and Y match MultiIndex A and B A:

You can first turn the ["TEST", "RECORDING"] columns of A into a pd.Index using .set_index, then use pd.Index.isin to find a mask representing the rows whose (TEST, RECORDING) pairs are in B.index, then negate the mask and index back A.

In short:

C = A[~A.set_index(["TEST", "RECORDING"]).index.isin(B.index)]

Output:

   TEST  RECORDING   FILENAME
4     3          1  ghjk.xlsx
5     3          2  vbnm.xlsx

Alternatively, if you are using Pandas 3.0+, you can use pd.DataFrame.merge with how="left_anti" (thanks to @sammywemmy):

C = A.merge(B[[]], how="left_anti", left_on=["TEST", "RECORDING"], right_index=True)

Where B[[]] is for selecting none of the columns except for its index.

Setup:

import pandas as pd

A = pd.DataFrame(
    {"TEST": [1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3],
     "RECORDING": [1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2],
     "FILENAME": ["qwer.xlsx", "asdf.xlsx", "zxcv.xlsx", "tyui.xlsx", "ghjk.xlsx", "vbnm.xlsx"]})

B = pd.DataFrame(
    {"STARTS": [1, 1, 2, 2],
     "ERRORS": [0, 0, 0, 0],
     "START RUN TIME": [0, 10, 20, 30],
     "END RUN TIME": [5, 15, 25, 35]},
    index=pd.MultiIndex.from_tuples([(1, 1), (1, 2), (2, 1), (2, 2)], names=["Test", "Rec"]))

Q: Obtaining mutable arrays from immutable A:

Originally i posed that question because of following problem: i needed performant hashtable for a codeforces problem, and to implement that i needed a function that works like Data.Array.accumArray, but also accumulates one global value, i provide signatures to make it more clear:

accumArray :: Ix i => (e -> a -> e) -> e -> (i, i) -> [(i, a)] -> Array i e
accumArrayExtra :: Ix i => (p -> e -> a -> (p, e)) -> p -> e -> (i,i) -> [(i,a)] -> Array i e

But in standard library there wasn't any function, that does that.

So i have written my own function with unsafePerformIO (for performance). But then i wondered, if it's able to realize it with pure functions and standard library, and actually i found the answer:

import Data.Array
import Data.Ix (Ix,range)
import Data.Array.Base (foldrArray)
import Data.Maybe (fromMaybe)
import Control.Monad (liftM2)
import Control.Arrow (first)


sndIndexes :: Ix i => (i,i) -> [i] -> Array Int Int
sndIndexes bs is = array (1,length is) $ foldrArray (++) [] $ (flip zip [1..] . reverse <$>) $ accumArray (flip (:)) [] bs $ zip is [1..]

prevs xs = Nothing : (Just <$> (init xs))

addToBottom3 (a,b) c = (a,(b,c))

accumArrayExtra :: Ix i => (p -> e -> a -> (p, e)) -> p -> e -> (i,i) -> [(i,a)] -> Array i e
accumArrayExtra f g l bs us = ans where
    ixs2 = elems $ sndIndexes bs (fst <$> us)
    go (hist, e) (u, (mbI', mbIx2')) = first (:hist) $ f (fromMaybe g $ liftM2 (!) ((arrStages!) <$> mbI') mbIx2') e u
    stages = accumArray go ([], l) bs $ zipWith addToBottom3 us $ zip (fmap fst <$> prevs us) (prevs ixs2)
    cnts = accumArray (\e _ -> e+1) 0 bs us
    arrStages = listArray bs [listArray (1, cnts!i) . reverse . fst $ stages ! i | i <- range bs]
    ans = snd <$> stages

So for example:

accumArrayExtra (\p e a -> (2*p, (p*a):e)) 1 [] (1,3) [(1,5),(2,7),(3,9),(1,1),(2,2),(3,3),(1,10),(2,11),(3,12)]

is

array (1,3) [(1,[640,8,5]),(2,[1408,32,14]),(3,[3072,96,36])]
